name: Bandipur
tagline: Car-free Newar bazaar on a ridge between Kathmandu and Pokhara
meta_description: Bandipur travel guide: the car-free Newar bazaar, Thani Mai sunrise, Siddha Gufa cave, heritage hotels and how to reach from Kathmandu or Pokhara.
summary: Bandipur is a preserved Newar trading town at about 1,030 m on a ridge above the Prithvi Highway, 8 km uphill from Dumre. Its main street is closed to cars and lined with 18th and 19th century brick houses. One night here breaks the Kathmandu–Pokhara drive with sunrise views, easy walks and Nepal's largest cave.
intro: Bandipur grew as a stop on the old trade route between India and Tibet. Newar merchants from Bhaktapur settled the ridge in the 18th century, and the town prospered until the Prithvi Highway was built along the valley floor in the 1970s and trade moved down to Dumre. Left behind, Bandipur kept what other hill towns lost: a single stone-paved main street of three-storey brick houses with carved wooden windows, small temples, a market square and a shady tundikhel parade ground at the end of the ridge.

Today the bazaar is closed to motor traffic, which makes it one of the most pleasant places in Nepal simply to walk. Old shops have become cafes, guesthouses and heritage hotels, but families still live above them and the town fills with local life in the evenings. On clear days from October to March the Himalaya stretches across the northern horizon from Dhaulagiri to Langtang, with Manaslu and Himalchuli prominent.

Bandipur is 143 km from Kathmandu and about 78 km from Pokhara, so it fits neatly into a road journey between the two. Most visitors stay one night: arrive in the afternoon, watch sunset from the tundikhel, climb Thani Mai hill for sunrise and walk down to Siddha Gufa before continuing. Two nights gives time for the village walk to Ramkot and a slower pace. Most of our road packages from Kathmandu to Pokhara include a Bandipur night for this reason.
facts: Car-free Newar bazaar, Thani Mai sunrise, Siddha Gufa cave

highlights.title: The car-free bazaar
highlights.text: Walk the stone-paved main street from the Bindebasini temple to the tundikhel. Look up at the carved windows and wooden balconies, the old library building and the shops selling local coffee and Bandipur oranges. The street is at its best in the early evening when families sit outside.

highlights.title: Thani Mai sunrise
highlights.text: A 30–40 minute climb from the bazaar leads to the small Thani Mai temple on Gurungche hill. At dawn you look over Bandipur's rooftops to a line of peaks from Dhaulagiri to Langtang, with the Marsyangdi valley still filled with cloud below.

highlights.title: Siddha Gufa
highlights.text: One of the largest caves in Nepal, about 437 m deep and 50 m high, reached by a steep 1–1.5 hour stepped trail down from the bazaar. Local guides with lamps lead you through chambers of stalactites. The path continues down to Bimalnagar on the highway.

highlights.title: Tundikhel viewpoint
highlights.text: The flat, tree-shaded ground at the north end of the bazaar was once where traders gathered before setting off for Tibet. Today it is a picnic spot and sunset viewpoint, with the Himalaya to the north and the valleys of Tanahun falling away below.

highlights.title: Khadga Devi and Bindebasini
highlights.text: Bindebasini, a two-tiered pagoda at the head of the bazaar, is the town's main temple. Khadga Devi, a short climb above, houses a sacred sword said to have been given by Shiva, shown only during Dashain. Both reflect Bandipur's Newar roots.

highlights.title: Ramkot village walk
highlights.text: An easy ridge walk of about 1.5–2 hours west leads to Ramkot, a Magar village of round, thatched and ochre-washed houses. Few tourists go, and the walk through orange groves and fields shows rural life a world away from the bazaar.

how_to_reach.text: From Kathmandu, follow the Prithvi Highway west for about 135 km to Dumre (4.5–5.5 h), then turn south up a winding 8 km road to Bandipur (20–30 min). From Pokhara, Dumre is about 70 km east (2–2.5 h). Tourist buses between Kathmandu and Pokhara stop at Dumre, from where local jeeps and taxis go up the hill. Cars park at the entrance to the bazaar; hotels send porters for luggage.

The old trade trail from Dumre climbs to Bandipur in about 2–2.5 hours, gaining roughly 600 m through villages and forest. From Bandipur you can also walk down past Siddha Gufa to Bimalnagar on the highway in about 2 hours and be picked up there.

where_to_stay: Stay in the bazaar itself to enjoy Bandipur after the day visitors leave. The Old Inn occupies two restored Newar townhouses on the main street, about 150 and 250 years old, with a back terrace facing the mountains; it is the address we use in most packages. Several smaller heritage guesthouses and family-run lodges line the same street, some with rooftop terraces, and there are a few resort-style properties on the ridge just outside the bazaar for travellers who want larger rooms and parking. Rooms in old houses are characterful but can be compact with steep wooden stairs, which matters for seniors.
tips: Arrive by mid-afternoon to see the sunset from the tundikhel and the bazaar's evening life.
Wear shoes with grip for the Siddha Gufa trail, which is steep, stepped and slippery after rain.
Book rooms early for October–November weekends, when Kathmandu families fill the heritage hotels.
Carry cash in Nepali rupees, as card machines are not reliable in small cafes and shops.
Ask your hotel to pack a light breakfast if you plan to climb Thani Mai before it serves food.

experiences.title: Bandipur heritage bazaar walk
experiences.summary: A slow walk with a local guide along Bandipur's car-free main street, from Bindebasini temple to the tundikhel, looking at Newar architecture, old trade houses, the library and temples. Ends at the viewpoint for sunset. Easy and flat, suitable for all ages.
body: The walk starts at Bindebasini temple, a two-tiered pagoda at the head of the bazaar with carved roof struts and a bell rung by every passing local. From here the main street runs about 500 m north along the ridge, paved with stone and lined with brick houses three and four storeys high. Your guide points out the details that mark Newar building: the latticed ankhi jhyal windows, the wooden lintels, the deep eaves and the ground-floor shopfronts with folding shutters that once sold cloth, salt and grain to caravans.

Halfway along, the Padma Library occupies one of the grander buildings, a reminder that Bandipur was an educated merchant town. Side lanes lead to small shrines of Ganesh and Narayan, to washing places fed by spring water and to courtyards where women dry chillies and grain. The guide explains how the town declined after the highway bypassed it in the 1970s and how the community chose in the 2000s to close the street to cars and restore the houses for tourism.

The walk ends at the tundikhel, the long flat ground at the end of the ridge, timed for sunset. On clear evenings the Himalaya turns orange from Dhaulagiri to Manaslu. Afterwards the bazaar fills with families, and cafes put tables on the street. Try local coffee grown on nearby farms, sel roti and a plate of Newar snacks before dinner. Our guide can also arrange a short visit to a local silk farm or a coffee grower near the bazaar on request.

faqs.q: Is Bandipur bazaar suitable for wheelchairs or seniors?
faqs.a: The main street is flat and paved with stone, so seniors can walk it comfortably at their own pace. It is uneven in places for wheelchairs but usable with help. Side lanes and the walks to Thani Mai and Siddha Gufa involve steep steps. Many old hotels have narrow wooden stairs, so ask for a ground-floor room.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for the Bandipur walk?
faqs.a: You can walk the bazaar on your own; it is small and safe. A guide adds the stories behind the houses, the trade history and the temples, and makes it easy to find side lanes and the library. In our packages a local guide leads the walk on the afternoon you arrive.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Bandipur?
faqs.a: Try Newar snacks such as bara (lentil patties), choila and beaten rice, local coffee grown around Bandipur, and seasonal oranges in winter. Cafes on the main street serve Nepali dal bhat and simple Indian and continental dishes. Vegetarian food is easy to find, and hotels cater for Jain diets with notice.

experiences.title: Siddha Gufa cave hike from Bandipur
experiences.price_hint: ≈ NPR 200–300 entry plus local guide fee
experiences.summary: A steep stepped trail down from Bandipur to Siddha Gufa, one of Nepal's largest caves at about 437 m deep and 50 m high. Local guides lead you through chambers of stalactites by lamp. Moderate fitness needed for the climb back.
body: Siddha Gufa lies below Bandipur on the hillside above Bimalnagar. From the bazaar a stone path drops steeply through forest and fields for about 1–1.5 hours, losing roughly 400 m of height. Near the entrance, a small ticket hut collects the fee and assigns a local guide, which is compulsory because the cave is dark and uneven inside. The guide carries a lamp; bring your own torch as a backup.

Inside, the cave opens into a high chamber about 50 m tall, with stalactites, stalagmites and flowstone formations named after gods and animals by local people. The full extent is about 437 m, and the visit takes 45 minutes to an hour, involving some scrambling over wet rock and a few ladders. Bats roost in the upper sections. Wear old clothes and shoes with good grip, as you will get muddy.

Returning to Bandipur means climbing back up the same steps, which takes 1.5–2 hours and is the hard part of the trip. Many visitors instead continue down to Bimalnagar on the Prithvi Highway in about 30–45 minutes and have their vehicle pick them up there, which works well on the day you leave Bandipur. The cave can be closed or slippery during heavy monsoon rain. Allow about four hours for the whole outing, and carry water and a snack, as there are only small stalls near the entrance.

faqs.q: How difficult is the Siddha Gufa hike?
faqs.a: The descent from Bandipur takes 1–1.5 hours on steep stone steps, and the climb back takes 1.5–2 hours, so moderate fitness and healthy knees are needed. Inside the cave there is some scrambling on wet rock. To avoid the climb back, walk down to Bimalnagar on the highway and meet your car there.

faqs.q: Is Siddha Gufa suitable for children?
faqs.a: Active children from about 8 years usually enjoy it, with an adult holding their hand on the wet sections. The steep steps and dark, slippery cave floor make it unsuitable for toddlers and anyone with mobility problems. Bring a head torch for each person and change of clothes for the drive.

faqs.q: Is a guide compulsory inside Siddha Gufa?
faqs.a: Yes. Local guides are assigned at the entrance and lead every group through the cave with a lamp, for a small fee on top of the entry ticket. They know the safe route over the wet rock and the names of the formations. Carry your own torch as a backup.

experiences.title: Thani Mai temple sunrise hike
experiences.image_query: Thani Mai temple Bandipur Himalaya view
experiences.summary: A 30–40 minute climb before dawn from the bazaar to the small Thani Mai temple on Gurungche hill, the highest point above Bandipur. Watch the sun rise over a line of peaks from Dhaulagiri to Langtang with cloud filling the valleys below.
body: Leave your hotel about 45 minutes before sunrise with a torch. The trail starts at the south-west end of the bazaar, passes the school and climbs steadily up a stone path through scrub and pine. It is short, about 30–40 minutes for most people, with a height gain of roughly 150–200 m. At the top, Thani Mai is a modest hilltop shrine of the mother goddess, with a few benches and prayer bells and an open view in every direction.

From here the Himalaya stretches along the northern skyline: Dhaulagiri, the Annapurnas and Machhapuchhre to the north-west, Lamjung Himal, Manaslu and Himalchuli straight ahead, and on very clear mornings Ganesh Himal and Langtang to the east. Below, the Marsyangdi and Seti valleys usually lie under a sea of morning cloud, with Bandipur's tiled roofs on the ridge in front of you. It is a favourite of photographers, who bring a telephoto lens for the peaks and a wide lens for the town below.

After the sun is up, return the same way for breakfast, or continue along the ridge towards the Khadga Devi temple. In March the hillside is covered with rhododendron and wild flowers. Avoid the climb in heavy rain, as the steps get slippery, and note that in the monsoon the view is usually lost in cloud. Local residents use the trail for morning exercise, so you will rarely be alone, and almost everyone who reaches the top rings the temple bell.

faqs.q: How long is the walk to Thani Mai?
faqs.a: About 30–40 minutes up from the bazaar for most adults, gaining roughly 150–200 m on stone steps and a dirt path, and 20–25 minutes back down. Children of about six and over manage it well. Allow two hours in total including time at the top for sunrise and photos.

faqs.q: Which mountains are visible from Bandipur?
faqs.a: On a clear morning you can see Dhaulagiri, Annapurna I and II, Machhapuchhre, Lamjung Himal, Manaslu, Himalchuli and Ganesh Himal, and sometimes Langtang far to the east. The view is clearest from October to February. From June to September cloud usually hides the peaks.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk to Thani Mai in the dark?
faqs.a: Yes, the trail is short, well used and close to town, and Bandipur is a safe, quiet place. Carry a torch or head lamp, wear shoes with grip and go in a small group. Your hotel can point you to the start of the path the evening before.

Yes, especially if you are driving between Kathmandu and Pokhara. It breaks a long journey with a night in a car-free Newar town, Himalayan sunrise from Thani Mai, and easy walks. It is quieter and more traditional than Pokhara. Skip it only if you are flying between Kathmandu and Pokhara and have very limited time.

faqs.q: How many nights should I stay in Bandipur?
faqs.a: One night is enough for the bazaar, sunset, Thani Mai sunrise and Siddha Gufa. Two nights lets you add the walk to the Magar village of Ramkot and enjoy the slow pace. Most of our Kathmandu–Pokhara road packages include one night here.

faqs.q: How far is Bandipur from Pokhara?
faqs.a: About 78 km: 70 km east along the Prithvi Highway to Dumre, then 8 km up a winding road to Bandipur. The drive takes 2.5–3 hours by private car. On a tourist bus, get off at Dumre and take a local jeep or taxi up the hill, about 20–30 minutes.

faqs.q: How far is Bandipur from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: About 143 km, a drive of 5–6 hours by private car via the Prithvi Highway to Dumre and then 8 km uphill. Road works and traffic around Naubise and Mugling can add time. You can combine the trip with Manakamana by cable car, whose base station at Kurintar is about 35 km before Dumre.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Bandipur?
faqs.a: October to March gives clear mountain views and dry, comfortable weather of 15–22 °C by day. December and January nights are cold, around 4–6 °C. April and May are warmer and hazier. During the monsoon from June to September the views are usually hidden and the trails slippery, though the town is green.

faqs.q: Can I bring my car into Bandipur bazaar?
faqs.a: No. The main bazaar is a pedestrian zone. Vehicles park at the entrance near the bus park, a few minutes' walk from most hotels, and hotels send staff to carry luggage. This is what keeps the street quiet and safe for children.

faqs.q: Is Bandipur good for families with kids?
faqs.a: Yes. The car-free street is safe for children to explore, the tundikhel is a good place to run around and Siddha Gufa is a real adventure for older children. Rooms in heritage houses have steep stairs, so families with toddlers may prefer a resort-style property just outside the bazaar.

faqs.q: Are there ATMs and Wi-Fi in Bandipur?
faqs.a: Wi-Fi is available in most hotels and cafes, though speeds vary. ATM access is limited and can be unreliable, so bring enough Nepali rupees from Kathmandu or Pokhara. Many small shops and cafes do not accept cards. Pokhara, about 2.5–3 hours away, is the nearest town with reliable banking.

faqs.q: Can I combine Bandipur with Manakamana and Gorkha?
faqs.a: Yes. Manakamana's cable car base at Kurintar is about 35 km east of Dumre on the same highway, and Gorkha is about 24 km north of Abu Khaireni, between Dumre and Mugling. A Kathmandu–Manakamana–Gorkha–Bandipur–Pokhara route over four or five days covers all three comfortably.
